name: The Einstellung Effect
statement: Prior problem-solving experience can blind people to simpler solutions, locking them into a familiar but suboptimal method.
meaning: The Einstellung effect describes a "mechanised state of mind" in which repeated use of one problem-solving method makes a person default to it automatically, even when a faster or better method is available. It reflects the negative influence of past experience, a mental set, on current problem-solving, and can occur regardless of intelligence.
mechanism: Repeated success with one procedure creates an automatised routine that is triggered whenever a superficially similar problem appears. This routine suppresses the active search for alternative, more efficient strategies because the familiar one already works. Time pressure and stress intensify the rigidity, while explicit prompts to look for a different approach can break it.

examples.text: In the Luchinses’ 1942 experiments, participants solved water-jar problems requiring a complex formula (B − A − 2C). When later given problems solvable by a much simpler formula, most kept using the complex method out of habit.

When experimenters told participants "Don’t be blind" before a solvable problem, over half of the previously rigid group switched to the simpler, more efficient solution — showing the effect is a bias, not an inability.

Summaries of the research report that rigidity rose to around 98% under time-pressure or stress conditions versus roughly 70% without such pressure, showing how anxiety strengthens reliance on the familiar method.

whyItMatters: It explains why experts and novices alike can miss obvious, better solutions once a routine is entrenched, with implications for education, chess, and organisational problem-solving, and it motivates deliberate strategies to counteract cognitive rigidity.
limits: The effect is not universal: a substantial fraction of Luchins’ participants found shortcuts unaided, and simple verbal cues can dissolve it. It is a bias in strategy selection, not a fixed deficit, and its strength varies with stress, age, and instructions.
misreadings: It is sometimes misunderstood as proof that expertise makes people worse problem-solvers in general, but it specifically describes a bias toward a previously reinforced method, not a loss of underlying ability.
origin: Named by psychologists Abraham S. Luchins and Edith Hirsch Luchins in their 1942 water-jar experiments; "Einstellung" is German for "setting" or "attitude."

sources.text: Einstellung effect, Wikipedia. — the definition, the Luchins 1942 water-jar experiments, and the "Don’t be blind" manipulation.
Abraham S. Luchins, Wikipedia. — his authorship of the water-jar studies and the Einstellung concept.
